title: Creative studio website — example plan
brief: An illustrative plan for a small creative studio that wants visitors to understand its work and make a qualified enquiry. These are example assumptions, not confirmed requirements for your project.
objective: Help a prospective client decide whether the studio fits their project and send a useful enquiry.
success: A visitor can identify the studio's service and find relevant work without assistance.
The enquiry flow explains the next step and preserves input if sending fails.

now: A clear introduction and services overview
An enquiry flow with confirmation and recovery
later: A journal, if the studio has capacity to maintain it
More case studies as evidence becomes available
out: A client portal or payment flow in the first release

context.detail: One person will maintain the site and project stories.
context.source: Illustrative scenario; confirm with the actual owner.

context.detail: The available brand assets, approved copy and case-study permissions still need checking.
There is no agreed launch date or budget yet.

steps.title: Agree on the visitor and goal
steps.summary: Choose the main audience and the action the site should help them take.
steps.why: This keeps the copy, page structure and feature choices focused on one useful outcome.
steps.deliverable: A short brief with audience, primary action and first-release scope.
acceptance: The owner can explain who the site serves and what visitors should do.
Assumptions and unresolved constraints are explicitly labeled.

steps.title: Prepare proof and project stories
steps.summary: Gather two project stories, real outcomes and approved imagery.
steps.why: Credible examples help visitors judge the studio; placeholder claims cannot do that.
steps.deliverable: Approved content and assets for two case studies.
acceptance: Each story explains the client's need, the work and the result.
The studio has permission to use the included images and claims.

steps.title: Map the path to an enquiry
steps.summary: Sketch the page structure and the journey from first visit to contact.
steps.why: It reveals missing information and confusing transitions before detailed design begins.
steps.deliverable: A small sitemap and a low-fidelity journey sketch.
acceptance: Services, relevant work and contact can be found from the main entry.
The mobile journey and unsuccessful submission state are included.

steps.title: Design and build the first version
steps.summary: Use the approved content and journey to create a coherent, responsive site.
steps.why: Using the real content and existing brand reduces redesign and arbitrary component choices.
steps.deliverable: A working local preview using the project's established stack and visual system.
acceptance: Desktop and mobile layouts preserve hierarchy and remain usable.
Forms, opened controls and keyboard focus follow the project design.
The enquiry path is tested without sending real messages.

steps.title: Verify the complete journey
steps.summary: Test the visitor's task and fix confirmed issues before choosing a release date.
steps.why: A successful build alone does not show that visitors can understand or use the site.
steps.deliverable: A review report with observed results, fixes and outstanding limitations.
acceptance: The main enquiry journey works with a keyboard and at a narrow viewport.
A failed submission keeps the entered information and offers a retry.
The owner reviews remaining issues and the actual publishing arrangements.

questions.question: Who needs to update the project stories?
questions.why: The update workflow affects the site's setup and maintenance cost.
questions.recommendation: Start with project files if updates are rare and you are happy to ask Pi to make them. Choose an editor if someone needs to publish independently.

options.label: Update through Pi and project files
options.benefit: A smaller setup with fewer services to maintain.
options.tradeoff: Changes need someone comfortable reviewing and publishing code.

options.label: Use a content editor
options.benefit: A non-developer can update stories independently.
options.tradeoff: Adds setup, permissions and maintenance work.

diagrams.title: From first visit to a useful enquiry
diagrams.description: An illustrative sitemap. The same places stay on the map while each layer explains a different part of the proposed site. These are planning choices, not a built website.

layers.title: Visitor journey
layers.description: Follow what a visitor sees and the choices they can make. Grey nodes belong to another part of the system.

nodes.summary: Understand the studio and its services.
nodes.detail: The first page should explain what the studio does, who it helps and where to find relevant work.
A short list helps visitors find work similar to the problem they need solved.

nodes.summary: See the need, work and outcome.
nodes.detail: A case study supplies evidence before the visitor decides to get in touch.
The form asks for enough context to start a conversation, with a clear explanation of what happens after sending.

edges.label: Explore work
edges.detail: The main page links to a small collection of relevant projects.

edges.label: Read a story
edges.detail: Choose a project to read its full explanation.

edges.label: Ask about a project
edges.detail: Visitors who already know what they need can contact the studio directly.

edges.label: Start a conversation
edges.detail: Each story offers a clear next step to discuss related work.

layers.title: What powers it
layers.description: Understand which parts are pages, content and server behavior. Specific products remain undecided until the existing project is inspected.

nodes.summary: A page built with existing components.
nodes.detail: Reuse the project’s navigation, content layout and visual tokens. The framework is a decision to confirm, not a new requirement.
Project files are the simpler starting option. A content editor is an alternative if a non-developer must publish independently.
The same layout displays each story’s title, images, explanation and outcomes. Content changes should not create a new page design.

nodes.summary: A branded form in the browser.
nodes.detail: Use the existing form components. Browser validation improves feedback, but the receiving server must validate submissions too.
This proposed endpoint receives the enquiry and forwards it using a delivery service chosen later. Service credentials stay on the server, outside the browser bundle.

edges.label: Provides project content
edges.detail: The collection supplies the data rendered by the reusable case-study page.

edges.label: Reuses navigation and controls
edges.detail: Shared components keep these pages consistent.

edges.label: Sends the enquiry
edges.detail: The browser calls the receiving endpoint; it does not hold delivery-service credentials.

layers.title: When something goes wrong
layers.description: Focus on the enquiry path. Other page nodes stay visible for orientation.

nodes.summary: Keep the draft and explain the problem.
nodes.detail: If submission fails, retain the entered information. Show a useful error beside the action and allow retry; do not display success without confirmation.
The endpoint reports whether it accepted the request. A network timeout can leave delivery uncertain, so the final implementation must choose how to prevent duplicate enquiries.

edges.label: Submit or retry
edges.detail: Retry should reuse the saved input and handle possible duplicate delivery.

edges.label: Accepted, rejected or uncertain
edges.detail: Translate the server result into a clear message the visitor can act on.
